case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court that had original jurisdiction over a case and stayed it pending arbitration under the FAA retains jurisdiction in that same still-pending case to decide post-arbitration motions (confirm/vacate/modify) without identifying a new, independent basis for federal subject-matter jurisdiction.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16 (especially §§ 3, 6, 9–11), and federal subject-matter jurisdiction statutes implicated by the parties’ arguments (28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1332, 1367) as interpreted in Supreme Court precedent (including limits on ancillary/supplemental jurisdiction).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that once the district court stayed an action pending arbitration, the court should be able to handle post-arbitration motions in the same case as a continuation of the original exercise of jurisdiction—i.e., the court retains jurisdiction and need not locate a separate, redundant jurisdictional hook. Petitioner emphasizes efficiency and the FAA’s procedural design (notably treating post-award applications as motions under FAA § 6), contends that requiring a new jurisdictional basis is formalistic and creates unnecessary duplication, and points out that multiple circuits have adopted the retention-of-jurisdiction view (arguing the Second Circuit’s contrary approach is wrong and creates a review-worthy split).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that FAA post-award proceedings are not automatically within federal jurisdiction simply because the original federal suit existed and was stayed; instead, a motion to confirm/vacate creates a distinct controversy requiring its own jurisdictional basis. They contend that confirming an award converts a private arbitral result into a federal judgment and is not the same as adjudicating the original federal claims, so 28 U.S.C. § 1331 does not supply jurisdiction. They further argue supplemental/ancillary jurisdiction is unavailable because the post-award dispute does not share the required factual common nucleus with the federal claims (invoking Kokkonen-type limits), and they stress that any circuit split is underdeveloped and this case presents vehicle concerns.
key_precedents: Hall Street Associates, L.L.C. v. Mattel, Inc.
Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of America
MasterCard Int’l Inc. v. Visa Int’l Service Ass’n (2d Cir.)
Harry Hoffman Printing, Inc. v. Graphic Commc’ns Int’l Union, Local 261 (2d Cir.)
Beijing Shougang Mining Inv. Co. v. Mongolia (2d Cir.)
Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co. (2d Cir.)
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc. (2d Cir.)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the best point that a § 3 stay keeps the case pending and § 6 contemplates post-award relief by “motion,” but that procedural continuity cannot do the work of subject-matter jurisdiction after Badgerow. Badgerow’s rule—that §§ 9–11 require an independent jurisdictional basis apparent on the face of the application—would be effectively nullified if a stayed federal docket could bootstrap jurisdiction for confirmation/vacatur of a purely state-law award dispute. As Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 6 is a manner-of-proceeding instruction “in the manner provided by law,” not a jurisdictional grant, and Kokkonen’s ancillary-jurisdiction carveout is limited to effectuating the court’s own judgments or expressly retained enforcement authority—neither of which is supplied by a non-merits § 3 stay. A narrow holding requiring an independent § 1331/§ 1332 basis for §§ 9–11 even after a § 3 stay best respects our precedents and keeps jurisdictional lines for Congress to adjust if it wishes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that a § 3 stay keeps the case pending and § 6 labels post-award requests as “motions,” suggesting the court is simply finishing what it paused. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 6 is a procedural instruction (“in the manner provided by law”) and cannot supply subject-matter jurisdiction that the FAA elsewhere does not confer; otherwise a stayed docket becomes a jurisdictional bootstrap that functionally nullifies Badgerow’s requirement of an independent jurisdictional basis for §§ 9–11 on the face of the application. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Kokkonen cuts the wrong way under its own logic: ancillary jurisdiction chiefly exists to effectuate a court’s own judgments or retained decrees, and a § 3 stay order is not a merits judgment to be enforced nor an incorporated settlement-like retention device. Efficiency and continuity concerns, though real as Justice Jackson notes, cannot overcome Article III and the statutory limits Congress enacted in §§ 1331 and 1332.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that a § 3 stay keeps the case “pending” and § 6 labels subsequent relief as a “motion”—does not satisfy Badgerow’s requirement that §§ 9–11 relief rest on an independent jurisdictional basis apparent on the face of the application. Calling something a “motion” and keeping a docket number open cannot do the jurisdictional work Congress reserved to §§ 1331 and 1332; otherwise, any party could “manufacture” federal enforcement jurisdiction by first filing a federal suit (or being compelled there) and then arbitrating, functionally nullifying Badgerow. Kokkonen, as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, allows ancillary jurisdiction chiefly to effectuate the court’s own decrees; a bare § 3 stay order is not a merits judgment and does not incorporate or retain enforcement authority over a later private award. Justice Jackson’s efficiency concerns are real, but under a textualist approach they are for Congress, not for us, to cure by implying post-award jurisdiction absent a statutory grant.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point is that § 6 is procedural and cannot “bootstrap” jurisdiction in a way that would undercut Badgerow, but that framing assumes the §§ 9–11 request is a freestanding new application rather than motion practice in a concededly live federal case. Kokkonen cuts against the Respondent here: its limit is about a court reaching beyond a terminated case, whereas a mandatory § 3 stay is an ongoing federal order that keeps the action pending and necessarily carries incidental authority to manage and conclude the stayed proceeding—including lifting the stay and resolving the award-related motions Congress channeled through § 6. Justice Alito’s characterization of confirmation/vacatur as a wholly new controversy ignores that the district court compelled arbitration and retained the case precisely to provide the limited judicial supervision the FAA contemplates, and forcing a redundant second jurisdictional showing predictably burdens weaker parties without advancing Article III values. Badgerow’s no-look-through rule remains intact because we are not using the underlying dispute to create jurisdiction; we are recognizing continuing jurisdiction over an undismissed action the federal court already properly possessed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that procedure cannot create subject-matter jurisdiction and Badgerow requires an independent jurisdictional basis for stand-alone §§ 9–11 applications; I agree with that as far as it goes. But their argument assumes the post-award filing is necessarily a new “application” rather than a § 6 “motion” within a concededly jurisdictionally proper case that remains pending because of a mandatory § 3 stay—so the court is not bootstrapping into federal court, it is exercising continuing authority to bring its stayed action to a final disposition. Justice Thomas’s Kokkonen analogy is less persuasive in this posture because Kokkonen concerned post-dismissal enforcement of a separate settlement absent retained authority, whereas a stay is an ongoing judicial order that keeps the case on the docket and anticipates return to court. Extending Badgerow to require a second, redundant jurisdictional hook after the court has properly taken and never relinquished jurisdiction reads the FAA’s integrated stay/motion structure in an unnecessarily formalistic way that the text does not compel.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett offer the best point for petitioner: a § 3 stay keeps the case pending and § 6 speaks in terms of “motions,” suggesting procedural continuation rather than a new action. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 6 is procedural (“in the manner provided by law”) and cannot do the jurisdictional work Congress reserved to § 1331/§ 1332; otherwise a stayed docket would become a bootstrap that functionally evades Badgerow’s requirement that §§ 9–11 relief rest on an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of the application. Kokkonen does not carry petitioner’s load because ancillary jurisdiction there is tied to effectuating a court’s own judgment or retained enforcement authority, and a bare § 3 stay is neither—confirmation/vacatur is a distinct request to transform a private award into a federal judgment. Efficiency concerns Justice Jackson raises are real, but under our precedents (Badgerow and Hall Street) and basic separation-of-powers principles, they are for Congress to address, not for us to infer jurisdiction from procedural posture.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett make the best case that a § 3 stay keeps the matter pending and that § 6’s “motion” language suggests procedural continuity, but that continuity cannot do the jurisdictional work Badgerow forbids. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas stress, Badgerow’s rule that §§ 9–11 require an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of the application would be substantially undermined if parties could “bootstrap” federal jurisdiction simply by filing (or being compelled) into federal court pre-arbitration and then returning post-award on the stayed docket. Kokkonen’s ancillary jurisdiction is aimed at effectuating the court’s own decrees; a § 3 stay is not a merits judgment or an express retention/enforcement order, so confirming/vacating a private arbitral award is not merely “managing” the court’s proceedings. The efficiency and fairness concerns Justice Jackson raises are real, but under an institutionalist approach they are for Congress to address rather than for us to create an implied exception that sits uneasily with Badgerow and Article III limits.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s best point is that § 6 is procedural and, under Badgerow and Kokkonen, cannot be used to “bootstrap” subject-matter jurisdiction for a §§ 9–11 request that would otherwise lack an independent jurisdictional basis. But that framing assumes the post-award filing is a freestanding new “application,” whereas in a § 3-stayed case the court’s Article III jurisdiction over the live action never lapsed; the court is exercising incidental authority to manage its own ongoing docket and to lift/modify its stay and enter final disposition. Kokkonen’s limit is keyed to a terminated case (dismissal) and the absence of retained authority; a § 3 stay is an extant court order that anticipates return, making confirmation/vacatur part of concluding the same case rather than converting an unrelated private dispute into a federal judgment. Badgerow is therefore distinguishable on its own terms (stand-alone post-award applications), and extending it to stayed cases would treat procedural posture—stay vs. dismissal—as jurisdictionally irrelevant despite its concrete effect on whether the federal action remains pending.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s central point—that § 6 is purely procedural and cannot confer jurisdiction, and that Badgerow requires an independent jurisdictional basis for §§ 9–11—does not, in my view, fit this posture. Here the district court already had undisputed subject-matter jurisdiction over the underlying federal action and never relinquished it because a § 3 stay keeps the case live; deciding the ensuing § 6 “motions” is best understood as an exercise of the court’s continuing authority to manage and conclude that pending case, not as conjuring jurisdiction over a new, freestanding controversy. Kokkonen, as Justice Thomas frames it, is materially different because it involved post-dismissal enforcement of a separate agreement; by contrast, a stay order is ongoing and anticipates return to court, making post-award review tightly connected to the stayed proceeding. While Justice Gorsuch worries this will “nullify” Badgerow, I read Badgerow as addressing stand-alone applications with no live federal case—not requiring a redundant second jurisdictional gateway once a properly filed federal action has been stayed rather than dismissed.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FAA “bestow[s] no federal jurisdiction” and requires an independent jurisdictional basis for post-award applications under §§ 9–11; Badgerow confirms that courts may not expand jurisdiction by look-through or other atextual devices in this context. A stayed merits case does not itself supply subject-matter jurisdiction to convert a private award into a federal judgment, and neither § 1331 nor § 1367/ancillary jurisdiction fits because the confirm/vacate dispute is not the adjudication of the original federal claim and does not share the requisite common nucleus, as Kokkonen emphasizes limits on ancillary enforcement jurisdiction absent a clear jurisdictional anchor. Treating post-award requests as “motions” under FAA § 6 is procedural and cannot create jurisdiction where Congress has not provided it. A narrow ruling requiring an independent jurisdictional basis for §§ 9–11 applications best preserves institutional legitimacy and aligns with our jurisdictional precedents.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAA is "something of an anomaly" that supplies procedures but not federal subject-matter jurisdiction, and nothing in 9 U.S.C. §§ 9–11 (read with § 6’s motion procedure) purports to let federal courts confirm/vacate/modify awards without an independent jurisdictional grant. Under Badgerow v. Walters, a court must find subject-matter jurisdiction for post-award applications on the face of the application itself, and the fact that the court earlier had jurisdiction over a stayed merits action does not create federal jurisdiction over a distinct post-award dispute that seeks to transform a private award into a federal judgment. Kokkonen v. Guardian Life confirms that ancillary jurisdiction is limited and cannot be assumed merely because a matter is related in a broad sense; here the § 9–11 controversy is not the adjudication of the original federal claim and thus cannot rest on residual “retained” power absent statutory authorization. Because the Constitution and Congress, not efficiency, define the jurisdiction of the lower federal courts, I would require a new, independent jurisdictional basis for the post-arbitration motions.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FAA does not itself confer federal jurisdiction, and §§ 9–11 authorize post-award relief only in a court that already has an independent jurisdictional basis; treating post-award applications as “motions” under § 6 cannot expand Article III or the statutory limits on subject-matter jurisdiction. Badgerow v. Walters reinforces that courts may not use jurisdictional shortcuts for FAA confirmation/vacatur proceedings, and the fact that the original action was stayed under § 3 does not transform the later request to convert a private award into a federal judgment into the same federal “case” for jurisdictional purposes. Nor does ancillary/supplemental jurisdiction supply the missing hook here: under Kokkonen v. Guardian Life, enforcement-type jurisdiction is tightly limited and does not extend to a distinct contract-like dispute over the award absent an express retention mechanism tied to a judgment or dismissal order. Practical consequences cannot override these jurisdictional constraints; if Congress wants automatic federal jurisdiction for post-award proceedings in stayed cases, it must say so.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When a district court with undisputed original jurisdiction stays (rather than dismisses) an action under FAA §3, the case remains pending, and the court retains the practical power to “manage [its] proceedings, vindicate [its] authority, and effectuate [its] decrees”—including resolving the FAA §9–11 post-award motions that §6 expressly channels as streamlined motions in the same action. Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary enforcement jurisdiction turned on a dismissal and the absence of a retained federal judgment to enforce; here, by contrast, the court’s stay preserves continuing jurisdiction over the still-live case and makes post-arbitration review the natural endpoint of the court-ordered pause, not a new freestanding controversy. Badgerow’s refusal to “look through” for an independent jurisdictional hook in standalone §9–11 applications does not require stripping jurisdiction from a court that never relinquished it and is completing the stayed federal action. Requiring a redundant new jurisdictional basis would impose needless procedural hurdles and costs that fall hardest on employees and other vulnerable litigants compelled into arbitration, undermining fair access to judicial review of potentially unlawful awards.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: When a district court properly exercises original jurisdiction over an action and then stays that same action under FAA § 3, the case remains pending; post-award applications filed on that docket under FAA § 6 are best understood as procedural continuations necessary to bring the stayed case to a conclusion, not as freestanding new “civil actions” requiring a new jurisdictional hook. Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary jurisdiction cut against creating jurisdiction after a dismissal, but they also recognize a court’s inherent power to manage and effectuate its own orders; deciding confirmation/vacatur motions following a § 3 stay fits that “manage proceedings/ensure effectuation” category far better than the post-dismissal contract-enforcement posture in Kokkonen. Badgerow’s refusal to “look through” for §§ 9–11 jurisdiction in stand-alone petitions does not answer what happens when the court already has jurisdiction over an extant case and is asked to resolve post-arbitration motions within it, and Hall Street’s description of §§ 9–11 as ‘streamlined’ motion practice (via § 6) supports that integrated, workable reading. Requiring a new independent jurisdictional basis in the same stayed case would be formalistic and disrupt the FAA’s coherent procedural design by forcing duplicative filings and potentially conflicting fora to complete one controversy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FAA is "something of an anomaly" that "bestow[s] no federal jurisdiction" and requires an independent jurisdictional basis, so §§ 9–11 cannot be entertained in federal court absent jurisdiction supplied by 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 or 1332 (Hall Street). A stayed case under FAA § 3 remains on the docket, but the post-award applications seek to convert a private arbitral result into a federal judgment and do not themselves arise under federal law for § 1331 purposes (Badgerow). Nor does ancillary/supplemental jurisdiction supply what the FAA withholds: under Kokkonen, enforcement-type proceedings require either an independent jurisdictional grant or an order that makes enforcement part of the court’s retained authority, and a bare § 3 stay does not suffice. Reading the statutes as written respects Article III limits and avoids judicially creating a freestanding federal forum for award confirmation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FAA is “something of an anomaly” that creates federal substantive rules but does not itself confer subject-matter jurisdiction, and after Badgerow v. Walters the Court must be careful not to invent jurisdictional shortcuts for §§ 9–11 that Congress did not provide. A post-award application to confirm/vacate/modify under §§ 9–11 seeks to transform a private arbitral result into a federal judgment and is not the same as adjudicating the stayed federal cause of action, so original § 1331 jurisdiction over the merits does not automatically carry over to the distinct post-award dispute. Nor does ancillary/supplemental jurisdiction solve the problem under Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of America: absent an order that makes enforcement of the award part of the court’s judgment or otherwise retains enforcement authority, the post-award fight resembles a new contract-based controversy rather than enforcement of the court’s own decree, and § 1367’s “common nucleus” is not satisfied merely because the arbitration arose from the same relationship. Given the jurisdictional limits emphasized in Badgerow and the restraint counselled by Kokkonen, the district court must identify an independent basis for federal jurisdiction before ruling on §§ 9–11 motions even when the case was stayed under § 3.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FAA’s text contemplates that post-award relief is sought by “motion” in the same court proceeding, 9 U.S.C. § 6, and § 3 requires a stay—i.e., the federal case remains pending rather than terminated—while arbitration is had. When a case is stayed (not dismissed), the court’s continuing authority to manage and conclude the pending action supplies the necessary incident-of-jurisdiction to resolve the parties’ post-arbitration motions without demanding a second, independent jurisdictional hook, consistent with the limited ancillary jurisdiction recognized in Kokkonen v. Guardian Life and Peacock. Badgerow v. Walters bars “look-through” jurisdiction for stand-alone §§ 9–11 applications, but it does not address (and should not be extended to forbid) the court’s ability to finish a case that properly began in federal court and was merely stayed under § 3. Requiring a new jurisdictional basis here would elevate form over the FAA’s procedural design and undermine methodological consistency with how we treat other post-stay proceedings in cases already within federal jurisdiction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Because the district court had undisputed original jurisdiction at the outset and entered a mandatory FAA § 3 stay (rather than dismissing the case), the federal action remained pending, and FAA § 6 contemplates that post-award applications proceed by “motion” in that same action rather than a new suit. Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary enforcement jurisdiction turned on the court having dismissed the case and not retained authority; here, the stay itself preserves the court’s control over the still-live case and makes post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur a procedural continuation necessary to “manage its proceedings” and effectuate its orders. Requiring a new, independent jurisdictional hook after a § 3 stay would create formalistic duplication and practical inefficiency inconsistent with the FAA’s structure in §§ 3 and 6 and Hall Street’s understanding that FAA motions “obviat[e] the separate contract action” otherwise required. Badgerow’s insistence on an independent jurisdictional basis for stand-alone FAA petitions does not compel a contrary result where the federal court never lost jurisdiction over the underlying case because it was stayed, not closed.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court that properly had original jurisdiction over a case retains jurisdiction—after staying the case for arbitration under the FAA—to decide post-arbitration motions (confirm/vacate/modify) within the same pending action without identifying a new, independent basis for jurisdiction.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. §§ 3, 6, 9–10; federal subject-matter jurisdiction statutes implicated include 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1332, and 1367 (supplemental/ancillary jurisdiction principles).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur is not automatically within the court’s continuing jurisdiction simply because the court once had federal-question jurisdiction over the underlying claims; instead, an application to confirm or vacate is a distinct proceeding requiring its own jurisdictional basis (e.g., diversity or a federal question apparent on the face of the confirmation/vacatur request), and neither § 1331 nor § 1367 supplies jurisdiction here because confirmation converts a private award into a federal judgment and is not part of the same Article III case-or-controversy/common-nucleus as the original federal employment claims; petitioner also invokes Kokkonen-style limits on ancillary enforcement jurisdiction and points to decisions (and oral-argument themes) suggesting the FAA’s ‘motion’ procedure streamlines process but does not create federal jurisdiction.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that because the district court had undisputed original jurisdiction at the outset and entered a stay (not a dismissal) pending arbitration, the case remained pending on the court’s docket, so the court retained jurisdiction to resolve the ordinary post-arbitration motions in that same action without forcing the parties to file a new lawsuit and re-plead jurisdiction; they contend the FAA contemplates streamlined motion practice for confirmation/vacatur and that requiring a new jurisdictional hook after a stay is formalistic, inefficient, and inconsistent with how federal courts manage stayed cases; respondents also downplay the split’s depth/quality and suggest the case has potential vehicle issues (including petitioner’s alternative merits arguments below).
key_precedents: Hall Street Associates, L.L.C. v. Mattel, Inc.
Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of America
Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co. (2d Cir.)
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc. (2d Cir.)
Beijing Shougang Mining Inv. Co. v. Mongolia (2d Cir.)
MasterCard International Inc. v. Visa International Service Association (2d Cir.)
Local/Union No. 2 United Ass’n of Journeymen (2d Cir.)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that the FAA supplies no freestanding jurisdiction and that Badgerow bars “look-through” for §§ 9–10 as standalone applications, but that point does not carry over cleanly where the district court already had undisputed original jurisdiction and never relinquished it. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, the procedural posture matters: a § 3 stay keeps the civil action pending, and § 6’s command that FAA applications be handled “as motions” is most naturally read to operate within that same pending case rather than require a new jurisdictional reboot. Kokkonen, which Thomas invokes, addressed enforcement after dismissal—i.e., after the court had terminated the case—and therefore does not compel treating post-award motions in a stayed case as a jurisdictionally new controversy. A minimalist holding limited to cases with valid original jurisdiction at filing and an actual § 3 stay (not a dismissal or equivalent) respects Badgerow’s baseline while preserving orderly administration of stayed federal cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the textual point that a § 3 stay keeps the original action pending and that § 6 says FAA applications “shall be made and heard… as motions,” so (they say) no new jurisdictional showing is needed. But § 6’s procedural instruction cannot enlarge the federal courts’ subject-matter jurisdiction: Badgerow’s core rule is that §§ 9–10 relief requires an independent jurisdictional grant, and treating confirmation/vacatur as a “motion” in a stayed case is still a request for a new federal judgment on a private award without Congress clearly authorizing jurisdiction for that post-award phase. Kokkonen reinforces that continuing/ancillary authority is limited and does not supply jurisdiction to enforce private agreements absent statutory authorization; a stay versus dismissal does not answer the threshold question whether the court has power to enter an award judgment when the underlying merits have been removed to arbitration. Under an originalist, textual reading, nothing in the FAA’s text clearly states that a § 3 stay preserves jurisdiction for §§ 9–10 in a way that overrides Badgerow’s insistence on an independent jurisdictional basis for the application itself.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that the FAA “bestow[s] no federal jurisdiction” and that Badgerow forbids looking through to the underlying merits, but those principles address freestanding §§ 9–10 proceedings, not the court’s power to complete a case it already properly has and has stayed rather than dismissed. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, a § 3 stay keeps the Article III case pending, and § 6’s instruction that FAA applications be handled “as motions” is best read to operate within that continuing action—so no new jurisdictional hook is being manufactured. Kokkonen, which Thomas invokes by analogy, involved a terminated case and a new contract dispute; here the post-award motion is the contemplated next step in the same federal action the court retained on its docket. Treating confirmation/vacatur after a § 3 stay as jurisdictionally separate would impose an atextual, formalistic trap without serving any meaningful limit on federal judicial power.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that the FAA does not itself confer subject-matter jurisdiction and that §§ 9–10 cannot be bootstrapped into federal court by “look-through” reasoning, but that premise does not answer the posture here: a § 3 stay leaves the original § 1331 case pending, so the court is not conjuring new jurisdiction so much as exercising continuing authority to bring the stayed action to judgment. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 6’s instruction that FAA applications proceed “as motions” makes most sense as motion practice in that same live case, and Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary jurisdiction are aimed at post-dismissal disputes where the court has relinquished the action entirely. Treating post-award confirmation/vacatur as requiring a brand-new suit after a mandatory stay would impose a formalistic hurdle with predictable, inequitable effects on employees and other vulnerable litigants, without a clear textual command to do so. Badgerow remains satisfied because we are not manufacturing jurisdiction from the FAA; we are relying on jurisdiction properly invoked at the outset and never terminated by dismissal.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press that § 6’s procedural “motion” label cannot itself create subject-matter jurisdiction and that Badgerow rejects look-through jurisdiction for freestanding §§ 9–10 applications. But that objection assumes the post-award request is a new action; as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, a § 3 stay leaves the original § 1331 case pending, so the court is exercising continuing jurisdiction over the same Article III “case” it already properly had, not manufacturing jurisdiction from the FAA. Kokkonen does not compel a contrary result because it addresses post-dismissal enforcement where the federal action has ended; treating a stayed case as jurisdictionally extinct would be both atextual (given § 6’s motion framework) and administratively unworkable in the FAA’s stay-then-motion scheme. A narrow holding limited to cases with undisputed original jurisdiction at filing and an actual § 3 stay respects Badgerow’s baseline while preserving coherent, workable federal procedure.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that the FAA creates no freestanding jurisdiction and that Badgerow forbids look-through for standalone §§ 9–10 applications, but that does not resolve the distinct posture where a court already has undisputed original jurisdiction and has entered (and maintained) a § 3 stay. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 3’s stay keeps the civil action pending and § 6’s direction that FAA applications be heard “as motions” most naturally treats post-award confirmation/vacatur as motion practice within the existing case, not a new suit requiring a fresh jurisdictional grant. Kokkonen, as Justice Alito notes, involved a dismissed case and a new contract dispute; here the court is finishing the very case it retained, so continuing jurisdiction is not “bootstrapped” from the FAA but carried forward from the original, properly invoked Article III jurisdiction. Limiting the holding to cases with an actual § 3 stay (not a dismissal or functional final judgment) respects Badgerow’s jurisdictional discipline while honoring the FAA’s text and procedural design.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that the FAA supplies no freestanding jurisdiction and that Badgerow bars look-through for standalone §§ 9–10 applications, but that principle does not answer the distinct posture here: the district court already had undisputed § 1331/1332 jurisdiction and, under § 3, the case remained pending. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 6’s instruction that FAA applications be made and heard “as motions” is best read as operating within that still-open civil action, not as authorizing (or requiring) a new lawsuit with a renewed jurisdictional hook. Kokkonen, which Thomas invokes by analogy, is materially different because it involved enforcement after dismissal—i.e., after the court relinquished the case—whereas a stay preserves the court’s ongoing authority to bring the same case to judgment. On an institutionalist, precedent-respecting view, we can cabin Badgerow/Hall Street by holding only that continuing jurisdiction exists when the original federal case remains live via a true § 3 stay, avoiding both jurisdictional bootstrapping and a formalistic trap.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that the FAA does not itself confer subject-matter jurisdiction and that procedure alone cannot create jurisdiction, but his framing treats the §§ 9–10 request as a new “case” rather than motion practice within an existing Article III case that was properly filed and never dismissed. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, a § 3 stay keeps the civil action pending, and § 6’s textual directive that FAA applications be made “in the manner provided by law for the making and hearing of motions” is best read to authorize post-award motions in that same case without a second jurisdictional pleading. Kokkonen’s ancillary-jurisdiction limits are triggered by dismissal and the resulting termination of the action; they do not compel us to treat a stayed case as jurisdictionally extinguished. Badgerow and Hall Street remain satisfied because we are not “looking through” to manufacture jurisdiction for a freestanding FAA proceeding—we are completing a still-pending case over which jurisdiction was properly invoked at the outset.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to insist that § 6’s “as motions” language cannot itself manufacture subject-matter jurisdiction, and that Badgerow/Hall Street reject any theory that the FAA is a freestanding jurisdictional grant. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the jurisdictional anchor here is not the FAA application viewed in isolation—it is the still-pending Article III case preserved by a § 3 stay, which keeps the court’s original § 1331/§ 1332 jurisdiction live rather than forcing a new civil action. Kokkonen’s caution about post-dismissal ancillary enforcement has less bite in this posture because there has been no dismissal relinquishing the case, and the post-award confirmation/vacatur step is the statutorily contemplated way to conclude the same stayed action. As a matter of procedural fairness and practical administration, I remain unpersuaded that Congress clearly required litigants to incur the jurisdictional and timing traps of refiling simply to obtain the end-of-case judgment that completes the stayed proceeding.

John Roberts.reasoning: Because the district court had undisputed original jurisdiction at the outset (28 U.S.C. §§ 1331/1332) and entered a stay under FAA § 3 rather than dismissing the action, the Article III case remained pending on the court’s docket, permitting the court to resolve the post-arbitration applications as motions within that same case under FAA § 6. That narrow holding is consistent with the FAA’s “streamlined treatment as a motion” (Hall Street) and avoids the formalistic inefficiency of requiring a new suit and re-pleading jurisdiction after a court-ordered stay. Kokkonen’s limitation on ancillary enforcement jurisdiction is distinguishable because it involved a terminated case (dismissal) and a new contract dispute, whereas here the court is completing the stayed federal case by acting on the arbitral outcome it ordered the parties to pursue. This approach hews closely to precedent (including Badgerow’s emphasis that the FAA itself does not create jurisdiction) by not recognizing free-standing FAA jurisdiction, but simply recognizing continuing jurisdiction in an already properly-invoked and still-pending action.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Federal courts possess only the jurisdiction Congress has conferred, and the FAA "bestow[s] no federal jurisdiction" but instead requires an independent jurisdictional basis for any application to confirm or vacate an award. Hall Street Associates, L.L.C. v. Mattel, Inc., 552 U.S. 576, 581–82 (2008); see also 9 U.S.C. §§ 9–10. A stayed merits action under 9 U.S.C. § 3 does not itself supply subject-matter jurisdiction over a later §§ 9–10 application, which is a distinct request to transform a private arbitral award into a federal judgment, and Badgerow v. Walters confirms courts may not manufacture jurisdiction by looking through to the underlying dispute. 596 U.S. 1 (2022). Nor does ancillary jurisdiction fill the gap absent a jurisdiction-retaining order of the kind discussed in Kokkonen, and in any event ancillary power cannot override the basic rule that jurisdiction must be grounded in statute. 511 U.S. 375, 377–82 (1994).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Because the district court had undisputed original jurisdiction at the outset (28 U.S.C. §§ 1331/1332) and entered a stay under FAA § 3 rather than a dismissal, the Article III “case” remained pending on the court’s docket; in that procedural posture, resolving §§ 9–10 confirmation/vacatur requests as “motions” under FAA § 6 fits within the court’s continuing authority to bring the stayed case to a final, enforceable disposition. Kokkonen limits ancillary jurisdiction after dismissal absent retention or incorporation, but it does not compel stripping jurisdiction where the court never relinquished the case through a final judgment and is merely completing the stayed proceeding. Badgerow and Hall Street correctly insist the FAA does not itself create jurisdiction, yet they do not require a court that already has jurisdiction and has stayed (not closed) the action to reestablish a new, independent jurisdictional basis before it can act on the post-arbitration motions that the FAA prescribes. As a practical matter, requiring a new lawsuit after a § 3 stay would create needless jurisdictional traps and delay enforcement, contrary to the FAA’s streamlined motion mechanism in § 6.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Because the district court had undisputed original jurisdiction at filing (28 U.S.C. § 1331) and issued a mandatory stay under FAA § 3 rather than dismissing, the Article III case remained pending, and the court could resolve the statutorily contemplated post-arbitration motions (9 U.S.C. §§ 9–10) within that same action without forcing a new jurisdictional pleading. Kokkonen limits ancillary jurisdiction after dismissal absent an express retention mechanism, but its logic cuts differently where the court retains the case on its docket via a stay and must manage completion of the dispute-resolution process it ordered, including entry of judgment on (or setting aside) the award. Hall Street and FAA § 6 contemplate “streamlined” motion practice in the existing case, and a contrary rule would create a procedural trap that disproportionately burdens employees and other vulnerable litigants by requiring duplicative filings and risking time-bar/fee barriers to vacatur or confirmation. Badgerow’s insistence that the FAA does not itself create jurisdiction is satisfied here by the already-existing jurisdictional anchor for the pending case, rather than a new, freestanding FAA action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Because the district court undisputedly had original jurisdiction at filing (28 U.S.C. § 1331) and entered a § 3 stay rather than a dismissal, the action remained pending on the court’s docket; in that posture, deciding the FAA §§ 9–10 applications “as motions” under § 6 is best read as a continuation of the same case, not a new freestanding civil action requiring a fresh jurisdictional showing. That reading fits the FAA’s streamlined, workable scheme and avoids the formalism Hall Street described—confirmation/vacatur motion practice that “obviat[es] the separate contract action” otherwise required—while remaining consistent with Badgerow’s insistence that the FAA does not itself create jurisdiction (the court here is not manufacturing jurisdiction, but exercising continuing jurisdiction in a case already properly in federal court). Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary jurisdiction are aimed at post-dismissal enforcement of settlements absent retention of jurisdiction; they do not compel a new jurisdictional inquiry where the court has not terminated the case but merely stayed it under § 3 pending completion of the arbitral process the court ordered. Requiring a new, independent jurisdictional basis after a stay would undermine the coherence and workability of § 3 stays and § 6 motion practice without any clear textual command to that effect.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The district court’s original jurisdiction over the action (28 U.S.C. §§ 1331/1332 as applicable) is not extinguished by a § 3 FAA stay; a stay presupposes the case remains pending, so the court retains authority to proceed to the case’s next step—resolving the FAA § 9–10 applications—without demanding a new, freestanding jurisdictional hook. Nothing in the FAA’s text purports to require a new civil action after a stay; to the contrary, § 6 directs that applications under the Act “shall be made and heard in the manner provided by law for the making and hearing of motions,” which naturally contemplates continuation within the same case. Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary jurisdiction concerned enforcement of a settlement after dismissal and the absence of retained jurisdiction; here there was no dismissal, and post-arbitration motions are part of administering the stayed case rather than a new controversy. Badgerow and Hall Street confirm the FAA does not itself create federal jurisdiction, but they do not compel treating post-stay confirmation/vacatur as a separate lawsuit when an Article III case properly invoked federal jurisdiction and remains on the docket under a statutory stay.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Because the district court undisputedly had original jurisdiction at filing (28 U.S.C. § 1331 or § 1332) and entered a stay under FAA § 3 rather than a dismissal, the Article III “case” remained pending on the court’s docket, and the court could exercise traditional ancillary/continuing jurisdiction to complete the matter by resolving the parties’ post-arbitration motions under FAA §§ 9–10 in the same action. Kokkonen’s limitation on ancillary jurisdiction principally addressed enforcement of a separate settlement after the underlying case had been dismissed without retained jurisdiction; here, by contrast, the stay preserves the court’s control over the ongoing action and the award-confirmation/vacatur motions are the FAA’s contemplated follow-on procedure (FAA § 6) to conclude the stayed case. Badgerow and Hall Street confirm the FAA does not itself create federal jurisdiction, but they do not require a new, freestanding jurisdictional basis when the federal court already properly has and continues to hold jurisdiction over a stayed case. As a practical matter and consistent with institutional concerns, requiring a new jurisdictional hook after a § 3 stay would be formalistic and unworkable, encouraging duplicative filings and undermining the FAA’s streamlined “motion” mechanism.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textually, the FAA contemplates that post-award relief proceeds by “motion” in the existing action (9 U.S.C. § 6), and when the district court enters a § 3 stay rather than dismissing, the civil action remains pending on the docket, preserving the court’s power to conclude what it began. Consistent with Kokkonen v. Guardian Life, ancillary jurisdiction extends to proceedings necessary to manage and effectuate the court’s orders; deciding confirmation/vacatur in the stayed case is closely tied to enforcing the stay’s premise that arbitration will resolve the dispute and that the court will thereafter take the statutorily prescribed next step. Badgerow v. Walters reinforces that the FAA itself supplies no freestanding jurisdiction, but it does not require a second, independent jurisdictional showing when the court already properly exercised original jurisdiction and never relinquished it by dismissal. Hall Street Associates underscores that § 6’s streamlined motion practice is meant to obviate a separate enforcement action, a reading best harmonized with retained jurisdiction after a § 3 stay.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Because the district court had undisputed original jurisdiction at filing (28 U.S.C. §§ 1331/1332) and entered a § 3 stay rather than dismissing the action, the matter remained the same pending “case” on the court’s docket, and the court may resolve the FAA §§ 9–10 post-arbitration motions as incident to concluding that stayed action under the FAA’s streamlined “motion” procedure (9 U.S.C. § 6). Badgerow v. Walters holds that the FAA does not itself supply jurisdiction and that jurisdiction must appear on the face of a standalone §§ 9–10 application, but it does not require a court to pretend a stayed, still-pending federal case has evaporated and then demand a new jurisdictional hook for what is functionally the case’s court-supervised completion. Kokkonen v. Guardian Life limits ancillary enforcement jurisdiction after a dismissal absent retained jurisdiction or incorporation, but here there was no dismissal and the court’s continuing control over its stayed case supports jurisdiction to enter the usual post-arbitration orders without forcing an inefficient refiling. This approach better serves procedural fairness and practical consequences by avoiding a jurisdictional trap for parties who followed § 3’s stay mechanism and then sought the FAA’s prescribed post-award relief in the same action.
